source.title_on_document: Writing, creativity, and artificial intelligence. ChatGPT in the university context

supplement.holds: The paper refers to no supplementary material. All statistics are in Tables 2-5 (PDF pp. 6-7, journal pp. 50-51).

paper_design_summary: Two designs. (1) Twenty free or freemium text-generation AI systems and 193 Spanish university students each completed Games 2 (uses of a rubber tube) and 3 (consequences of people never stopping growing) of the PIC-A creativity test; AI output and the students' unaided output were compared on fluency, flexibility, and narrative originality with Mann-Whitney U tests. (2) In the same one-hour session, the same students then redid both games with ChatGPT's help, improving their first answers; pretest and posttest scores were compared with Wilcoxon tests in a one-group pretest-posttest design with no control group and no random assignment.

studies.label: AI systems versus unaided students on PIC-A Games 2 and 3

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned. Output of 20 AI systems is compared with the unaided (pretest) output of 193 students.
assignment.quote: a descriptive and comparative non-experimental or ex post-facto quantitative research study was carried out, in which the level of creativity achieved by both the AI systems and the students was analysed

arms.name: AI systems
arms.description: 20 LLM text-generation systems (19 with OpenAI/GPT-3 technology plus Dupla.ai); each prompted with the game instruction three times in a row, at first access

arms.name: Students (pretest, no aid)
arms.description: 193 university students who played the two games without any aid, 10 minutes each

participants.exclusions: No exclusions are described. Tables 4 and 5 do not print the number of observations; 193 is the sample size stated in Section 2.2. The AI side is 20 systems, not people.
participants.who: 153 women and 40 men aged 18 to 50, enrolled in Primary Education (degree and master's) at University of Murcia, Fine Arts at University of Salamanca, and Audio-visual Communication and Journalism at Miguel Hernández University of Elche; non-probabilistic convenience sample
participants.quote: 193 students (153 women and 40 men) aged 18 to 50 years old ... participated in the study. A non-probabilistic, purposive, convenience sampling procedure was used.

ai_tool.name_model: 20 systems listed in Table 1: ChatGPT, Copy.ai, Rytr, Peppertype, Copysmith, Jasper, Writesonic, Youchat, Anyword, ASKtoAI, Contentbot, Copymatic, Dupla, Magic Write (Canva), Neuro-Flash, Nichesss, ReAI, Simplified, Unbounce, Wordtune
ai_tool.how_used: The AI systems produced the answers on their own (no human involved); the instruction was typed in and the response collected, three continuous requests per game.

task.description: PIC-A (Creative Imagination Test for Adults) Game 2: list uses of a rubber tube (alternate uses). Game 3: what would happen if people never stopped growing (consequences).
task.duration: Students: 10 minutes per game, per the manual. AI: three continuous requests instead of the time limit.

outcomes.question: none

outcomes.name: Game 3 flexibility

outcomes.question: none

contrasts.reported: Human M 9,35 SD 8,509; AI M 7,80 SD 7,818; U 1644,500; Z -1,090; p ,276; Effect size .075 (students higher in mean, not significant)

studies.label: Students' pretest (no aid) versus posttest (with ChatGPT), one-group pre-post

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was randomized. All students did the games first without aid, then again with ChatGPT in the same session; the order was fixed.
assignment.quote: a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest study was carried out, where the creativity indicators obtained by the students, both before and after a learning intervention with the help of ChatGPT, were evaluated and compared.

arms.name: Pretest (no aid)
arms.description: Students played Games 2 and 3 without any aid, 10 minutes each

arms.name: Posttest (with ChatGPT)
arms.description: After registering in ChatGPT and trying test queries, the same students redid both games with ChatGPT's help, told to improve the content they wrote in the pretest

participants.exclusions: No exclusions are described. Table 5 does not print the number of observations; 193 is the sample size stated in Section 2.2.
participants.who: 153 women and 40 men aged 18 to 50 in education, fine arts, and audio-visual communication and journalism programs at three Spanish universities
participants.quote: Similarly, 193 students (153 women and 40 men) aged 18 to 50 years old ... participated in the study.

ai_tool.how_used: Students could ask the chat anything to improve their pretest text, including pasting the test instruction literally.

task.description: PIC-A Game 2 (uses of a rubber tube) and Game 3 (what would happen if people never stopped growing); posttest was a revision of the pretest answers with ChatGPT.
task.duration: One-hour session per group; pretest 10 minutes per game; posttest duration not stated

company_involvement.description: Funded by Spanish research project PID2020-113731GB-I00 (MCIN/AEI); no company involvement stated.

eligibility.reason: No random assignment: S1 compares output of 20 AI systems with unaided student output (ai_vs_human context), and S2 is a one-group pretest-posttest of 193 students with a fixed order (no AI first, then ChatGPT) and no control group (quasi_people, folded into observational). 193 students is the stated sample; the tables print no n and no exclusions are described.

one_line_finding: In a one-group pre-post design, 193 Spanish university students scored higher on PIC-A Game 2 fluency (10.47 to 13.08, effect size .408), flexibility (7.56 to 8.33) and narrative originality (11.02 to 14.45) and on Game 3 fluency when revising with ChatGPT, while 20 AI systems outscored the unaided students on Game 2 but not Game 3 (PDF p. 7, Tables 4 and 5).
open_questions: Context class: S1 is ai_vs_human and S2 is quasi_people (observational); the form allows one context_class and I chose observational because S2 is the study with people using AI. Holzner et al. (2025) used the ai_vs_human comparison.

Does the posttest-versus-pretest contrast belong on the site as observational context, given that the posttest is a revision of the pretest answers with extra time and no control group (codebook section 13, third open question)?
notes: Tables print Spanish decimal commas (e.g., 10,47); the reported strings keep them. The effect-size column in Tables 4 and 5 is not defined (likely r from Z, not stated). The 'b' superscript on the Table 5 Z values has no visible footnote in the PDF. The Results text (PDF p. 6) gives AI means M=15.54, 9.75, 11.15 (Game 2) and 13.78, 8.75, 8.12 (Game 3), which do not match Table 2 (29,3; 12,35; 37,4; 10,65; 6,90; 7,80); these text values appear to be the manual's reference means, but the paper attributes them to the AI systems' means ambiguously. Each AI system was prompted three times per game; how the three responses were combined into one score is not stated. Who scored the outputs and whether scorers were blind is not stated. Table 3 also gives student means by gender (M/W).
